newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CENTRAL BANKER FRANCO ON THE WAY UP.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CENTRAL BANKER FRANCO ON THE WAY UP.

text.p: Diminutive yet pugnacious, Gustavo Franco promises to bring to the role of Brazilian Central Bank chief a more fiery style than his predecessor Gustavo Loyola, who shunned the limelight.

With smooth passage through the Senate of his nomination as the next president of the Central Bank and reports he will assume office in a swank ceremony in the Presidential Palace, possibly on Thursday, Brasilia is already begining to speculate on how far he might rise politically.

"Some believe the pomp and circumstance surrounding Franco's appointment is also a signal he is being groomed to occupy one of the economic cabinet posts," wrote Correio Braziliense economic columnists Vicente Nunes and Regina Pires indicating that this may be just the starting point for Franco's political rise.
But how long the 41-year-old economist's star will continue to shine so brightly is anyone's guess.

For the moment, political analysts say, Franco's easy passage through the Senate -- far less turbulent than most Brasilia watchers had expected -- showed he had the stomach and the political savvy needed to run the Central Bank presidency.
Senators voted 56-10 Tuesday to approve Franco's nomination.
The Harvard-trained economist was one of the creators of the central plank of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's platform, the three-year-old "Plano Real" economic stabilization plan.
Using tight monetary policies and a strong reais currency to stabilize Latin America's largest economy, the plan managed to bring chronic hyperinflation down to 10 percent last year.
Franco is one of the few from the original Plano Real team to remain. Others, like Persio Arida and Edmar Bacha have fled to lucrative consultancies in the private sector.

As International Affairs Director of the Central Bank, Franco spearheaded Brazil's return to international money markets, which culminated recently in a well-received $3.0 billion global bond tied to a Brady debt buyback and swap.

His promotion is regarded by economists and political analysts as a victory for Finance Minister Pedro Malan against the proponents of looser monetary policies and a devaluation of the real, which some economists say is 20 percent overvalued.
In a hearing before the Senate Economic Affairs Committee last week, Franco defended the strong reais currency. He said tight money was essential to keeping inflation under control.

He also enjoys the wholehearted support of President Cardoso, which should serve him well if Congress decides to turn its wrath on the Central Bank for ignoring calls for more spending in presidential election year 1998.
Central Bank sources say Franco has been instructed to tone down his usual outspokenness now that he is in charge.
But he can be expected to continue to pour out high-browed essays, which he uses to keep the market abreast of his views and as a subtle way to float new ideas.
"My one vice is writing," Franco told senators last week. "I think this is the best way to develop one's ideas. I hope I shall be able to continue to work like this in the future."
